Compute deletes the draft lines and runs the structure's rules in sequence (Chapter 19). Drafts also refresh by themselves when a wage changes or a leave is approved.

p: Chapter 15 · Pay runs and payslips
x: Each payslip shows its problems as a banner and a badge: red (blocked) or orange (read it first). Validation also refuses if a dashboard warning marked block payslips concerns these payslips. Common pitfall: a banner that is not an error Emma's termination payslip shows "Payslip period does not match payrun": it covers 31 October only. That is expected for exit payslips (Chapter 17). Read each warning; do not try to make every banner disappear.

p: Chapter 15 · Pay runs and payslips
x: Validate is the point of no return of a payroll month. Before it, payslips are drafts that change with the data. After it, they are the official record of what each employee was paid: the amounts are frozen, and three things start. ValidateAny blocking warning or error? yes → refused, with the list of warnings to fix → A journal entry is created in draft, ready to post (Chapter 16) The payslip PDFs are generated and sent to employees, if the company setting says so The Pay button appears, to pay the net by bank file (Chapter 16) A validated payslip is never recomputed. If its data changes later, Odoo flags it as outdated and offers a correction.

p: Chapter 15 · Pay runs and payslips
x: A payslip needs a correction when what it says is no longer true. That happens more often than mistakes in the rules: information came late: a sick day or an unpaid day approved after the month was validated; a change was backdated: a raise agreed in March, effective from 1 January; the data was wrong: a wrong wage, a forgotten input, the wrong pay category; the law changed retroactively: a new rate published in July, valid from January (Chapter 11). A validated payslip has already been sent to the employee, booked in the accounts and counted in the declarations, so payroll never edits it. It cancels it with a negative copy and issues the right one; only the difference between the two is still to pay or to recover. Still a draft? Fix the data and press Compute again. Nothing was sent yet, so nothing needs undoing. Already validated or paid? Press Correct. Odoo creates a correction run with two payslips: Refundthe original, negated−2,614.27 + Correctionrecomputed with the right data2,537.30 = Differencestill to settle−76.97 Mélanie's January, after a late unpaid day (Mission 15.2) Three other tools exist for other situations: delete a draft payslip that should not exist; cancel a validated one that should never have existed (payroll managers only; its entry is reversed); and use an off-cycle payslip on another structure for a payment outside the regular month, such as a 13th month, holiday pay, an advance or a leaver's exit pay. The Payslip Correction wizard, opened from the Manage Payslip link of Mélanie's January payslip. ① the payslips affected by the change. ② Correct: a refund of the original and a recomputed payslip. ③ Revert only: the refund alone. ④ Keep it as is: Odoo stops flagging this payslip as outdated. Worked example: Mélanie's late unpaid day (Mission 15.2) Mélanie's unpaid day of 23 January is approved after January was validated. Her payslip shows an issue with a Manage Payslip link, and Correct creates a run Correction (01/26) Monthly Pay (BE): Payslip Net (€) Refund: Mélanie, January (the original, negated) −2,614.27 Correction: Mélanie, January (with the unpaid day) 2,537.30 Difference −76.97 The unpaid day removes one day at the fixed hourly rate (Chapter 14): basic 3,815.39 €. The run that Correct created. ① its name, Correction (01/26) Monthly Pay (BE). ② the correction payslip: 21 paid days, basic 3,815.39 €. ③ it carries the issue until it is validated. ④ the refund: −22 days, −4,000.00 € basic. The footer is the net effect: −184.61 € of basic wage. Common pitfall: validating a Belgian correction run The Belgian localization marks a payslip with a negative net as Paid at once, so Validate on the correction run fails with "You can't create a journal entry for a paid payslip". Validate the correction payslip itself. Around the world Belgium: ten structures (monthly pay, double holiday pay, 13th month, termination fees, exit holiday pay…). Luxembourg: a gratification and a 13th month. Mexico: a Christmas bonus. Saudi Arabia: a salary advance and loan structure. Most others: one regular structure. In practice: three checks before Validate Headcount: one payslip per person you expect (Yannick from March, Emma's exit payslips in October). Delta: compare net and total cost with last month; explain every difference by an event. Issues: open every orange or red badge and read it.

p: Chapter 15 · Pay runs and payslips
x: A pay run is a period, a structure and a list of versions; its state follows its payslips (Draft, Ready, Done, Paid). Generating creates one draft payslip per valid version, with worked days; Compute adds the lines; Validate locks them and creates the journal entry. Issues and blocking warnings decide whether a payslip can be validated; banners are information, not always errors. A validated payslip is never edited: Correct creates a refund and a recomputed payslip in a correction run. Holiday pay, bonuses, advances and exit pay are off-cycle payslips on their own structures.

p: Chapter 16 · Accounting and payment
x: From payslip lines to one balanced entry, then to a bank file Explain how validated payslips become a journal entry, and which settings shape it Read a real payroll entry line by line and check that it balances Use the Adjustment Entry line as a configuration smoke test Pay a pay run with a SEPA file, and know what Paid does and does not mean in accounting Chapter 8 drew a payroll month as T-accounts on paper. Here Odoo does it: the structure and its rules hold the configuration, Validate triggers the entry, and a bank file pays the net.

p: Chapter 16 · Accounting and payment
x: Validating the payslips is not the end of the month. Two things still have to happen in the real world, and Odoo handles both: Book it. The company records in its accounts what the month cost and what it now owes, and to whom: the employees, the social security office, the tax office. That record is a journal entry. Pay it. The company sends the money. For the employees' net pay, Odoo produces a bank file the bank executes in one go. Book it Payslips validated → Journal entry created, in draft → The accountant checks and posts it Pay it Pay button on the run → Bank file (SEPA) → The bank pays each employee Both meet on the bank statement: the payment is matched with the net pay owed in the entry, and the debt is closed.

p: Chapter 16 · Accounting and payment
x: Four settings decide what the journal entry looks like. They are easiest to understand on the result, a simplified version of MyVidangeCompany's February entry: 1Journal: Salaries (SLR) · entry SLR/2026/02/0001 · 4one entry for the whole run 2Account 3Partner Debit Credit 620200 Remuneration 18,800.00 621000 Employer contributions 4,626.76 454000 Social security office the social security office 6,975.21 453000 Taxes withheld the tax office 3,978.86 455000 Remuneration owed 12,450.89 … The journal is the book the entry is written in; payroll has its own, Salaries. You set it on the structure. A structure without a journal produces no entry at all, and no error. The accounts are the lines of the company's chart of accounts: an expense (Remuneration) or a debt (Social security office). Each salary rule says which account its amount goes to: a debit account for what the company spends, a credit account for what it owes. The partner says to whom a debt is owed. It is also set on the rule. One entry per run, or one per payslip. The company setting Anonymize Journal Entries (Chapter 12) groups the whole run into one entry, so individual salaries cannot be read in the books. With the Belgian chart of accounts, the localization fills all four for you: the Salaries journal, the rule accounts and the anonymized entries.

p: Chapter 16 · Accounting and payment
x: The entry is created the moment the run is validated, in four steps: 1Collectthe lines of the validated payslips that have an account → 2Groupone entry per run (or per payslip), amounts summed per account → 3Balanceif debits ≠ credits, an Adjustment Entry line fills the gap → 4Waitin draft, dated the end of the month, for the accountant to post Step 3 matters most: Odoo never refuses an unbalanced entry, it quietly balances it. The next section shows why that line is a warning sign.

p: Chapter 16 · Accounting and payment
x: Accounting > Journal Entries > SLR/2026/02/0001, the entry of the whole February run (posted, dated 28 February). Debits and credits both total 23,426.76 €. p: Chapter 17 · Reports, declarations and a leaver
h: Why payroll reports to the authorities
x: An employer that runs payroll holds money that is not its own: the tax and the contributions it kept back from every payslip. The authorities need to know how much it kept, for whom, and when it pays it over. Employees need it too: their pension, unemployment and health rights, and their own tax return, depend on what the employer declared. So every country asks for reports. The names change from country to country; the four kinds below do not. Hire and exit notices Social security knows who is insured from the first day, and undeclared work becomes visible. BelgiumDimona, before the first hour of work ElsewhereHong Kong IR56E and IR56F; Türkiye’s hiring notice Periodic tax return The employer pays over the tax it withheld, and says how much. Belgiumform 274, every month ElsewhereUS form 941 (quarterly); Philippines 1601-C (monthly); India’s quarterly tax-at-source statement Periodic social security return Contributions are paid, and each worker’s pay and time is recorded for their future rights. BelgiumDmfA, every quarter ElsewherePhilippines SSS file; Kenya’s pension and health sheets; Switzerland’s ELM transmission Yearly certificate per employee The employee and the tax office see the year’s pay and tax, for the personal tax return. Belgiumform 281.10 ElsewhereUS W-2; Philippines 2316; Hong Kong IR56B; Kenya P9 A few countries go further and receive payroll as it happens: Mexico wants one signed electronic payslip per payslip, Australia a report to the tax office at every pay run. The idea is the same; only the rhythm changes (Chapter 7).

p: Chapter 17 · Reports, declarations and a leaver
x: Every declaration in Odoo, whatever the country, is a declaration sheet for one period. You create it, and Odoo does the rest in a fixed order: 1Createa sheet for the period and the company → 2PopulateOdoo finds the employees paid in the period → 3Computeit adds up their validated payslips, box by box → 4Checkit lists what the authority would reject → 5Generatethe file or the PDFs you submit The framework provides this design once; each country adds its own boxes, file format and checks. Key idea: a form is a sum of categories A declaration rarely looks at individual rules. It sums salary rule categories over the period: taxable base, withholding, contribution base. If a rule sits in the wrong category, the payslip can be right and the return wrong. Designing categories is designing the declarations (Chapters 20 and 22).

p: Chapter 17 · Reports, declarations and a leaver

Before the runall month long Record the events: hires, raises, time off, departures (Ch. 13, 14). Why first: the payslips are computed from them. Pay runa few days before payday Generate and compute the run (Ch. 15). Review warnings, the change against last month, the reports. Validate: the amounts are now final. p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
x: What goes into a payslip, what comes out, and the short loop in between Say in one sentence what the payroll engine does Name what goes into a payslip and where its lines go afterwards Read the engine's core loop and explain why it is the same in every country Name the five records you work with, who owns each, and how often each changes Tell which records ship with a country module and which belong to the customer Mélanie's February payslip has 44 lines; Marie's, on the same structure, has 49 (her car, her meal vouchers). A Mexican weekly payslip looks nothing like either. Yet nobody wrote a "Belgian payslip program" or a "Mexican" one. One small engine read a list of rules and applied them, one after the other. This part of the book explains that engine at the level you need to create payroll records and to review them.

p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
x: The payroll engine is the part of Odoo that turns one employee's data for one period into payslip lines. It takes the rules of one structure and applies them, in order, to the employee's contract terms, time and inputs. Three things follow from that definition: The engine knows no country. Everything a law says is in the rules and their parameters, which are data. The engine only runs them. The engine decides nothing. Whether a line appears, and how much it is, is decided by a rule. When a payslip is wrong, the cause is a rule or the data it read, almost never the engine. It runs again on demand. A draft payslip is recomputed whenever you click Compute or its data changes. A validated payslip is frozen (Chapter 15). What goes in The versionwage, family situation, structure type Mélanie: 4,000.00 €, single Timeschedule, attendance, overtime, time off → work entries → worked days February: 20 days, 152 h Inputsamounts typed for this period: a commission, an advance, a deduction → The engine 1Choose a period1–28 February 2026 2Choose a structurethe default of the version's structure type: Monthly Pay 3Compute the worked daystime becomes days, hours and amounts per time type 4Compute the rules, in ordereach rule may add one line, and its total to running totals → What comes out Payslip linesBasic 4,000.00 Social security −522.80 Withholding tax −826.69 … Net 2,614.27 Accountingone journal entry per run (Ch. 16) Declarations, reportssums of lines over a period (Ch. 17) Read the figure from left to right. On the left, the three kinds of data a payslip needs: who (the employee's version, Chapter 13), how much time (Chapter 14) and what else happened this period (inputs). In the middle, the four steps of the engine; Part III showed the first three, this part explains the fourth. On the right, the lines, and everything that reads them later: the journal entry, the declarations, the reports. Nothing downstream recomputes anything; it reads the lines. In practice When a payslip looks wrong, follow the figure from the left: is the version right (wage, situation, structure type)? Are the worked days right? Are the inputs right? Only then open a rule. Most "rule bugs" are data in one of the first three.

p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
h: Why a payroll engine at all?
x: Payroll law differs in every country and changes every year. If each country's payslip were a program, every new tax table would be a code change, and every customer who pays a sector bonus would need a developer. Odoo takes the other road: rules are data. A salary rule is a record: a name, a code, a condition and a small formula, usually a few lines of Python. Country modules ship their rules in data files; a customer can create more from the screen. One engine evaluates all of them the same way, giving each rule a dictionary of what it may see: the version, the worked days, the totals so far (Chapter 19 lists them). Here is that engine, simplified to its core: def compute_lines(payslip): seen = payslip._get_localdict() # what a rule may read lines = [] for rule in sorted(payslip.struct_id.rule_ids, key=lambda r: r.sequence): if not rule._satisfy_condition(seen): # condition false: no line at all continue amount, quantity, rate = rule._compute_rule(seen)[:3] total = amount * quantity * rate / 100 seen['result_rules'][rule.code] = {'total': total, 'amount': amount} rule.category_ids._sum_salary_rule_category(seen, total) # running totals lines.append({'code': rule.code, 'amount': amount, 'quantity': quantity, 'rate': rate, 'total': total}) return lines For each rule, in order: test the condition; if it holds, compute an amount, a quantity and a rate; multiply them into a total; remember the result for later rules; add it to the rule's running totals (its categories, Chapter 20); keep one line. The real method, _get_payslip_lines, adds batches of payslips, year-to-date sums and a few hooks for countries, but the whole engine fits on one page; the names may change, the loop does not. That is why you can review any country's payroll once you can read its rules. line total = amount × quantity × rate ÷ 100 Mélanie's social-security line: amount 4,000.00 € (her contribution base), quantity 1, rate −13.07 %, total −522.80 €. Key idea The engine is small and stable; the rules are many and change every year. Everything in this part is about reading and placing rules, because that is where every country's law lives.

p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
h: The five records you work with
x: Five kinds of record decide how a payslip is computed. Chapter 12 introduced four of them by following Mélanie's payslip; here they are side by side, with who owns them and how often they change. Structure type The kind of pay: who is paid how, and how often. Set on each employee's version; names the default structure. Ownercountry module; the customer picks one per version Changesalmost never ExampleBE CP200 BE; MX Employee Structure A named list of rules for one kind of payslip (Chapter 19). Ownercountry module; a customer may add one Changeswhen a new kind of payslip is needed ExampleBE Monthly Pay, 13th Month; MX Christmas Bonus Salary rule One line of the payslip: when it applies, how much, which totals it feeds (Chapter 19). Ownercountry module; customers add their own, such as a company allowance Changeswhen the law's method changes ExampleBE ONSS; MX ISR Salary category A named running total that rules add to and later rules read (Chapter 20). Ownercountry module Changeswhen the law creates a new base ExampleGROSS, NET; MX SBC Rule parameter A legal number or table with its dated values: rates, caps, tax scales (Chapter 21). Ownercountry module; Odoo adds the new values, not the customer Changesevery year, sometimes several times a year ExampleBE professional-expenses cap: 5,930 in 2025, 6,070 in 2026; MX l10n_mx_uma Two more long-lived concepts surround them: the employee's version, which the customer fills in (Chapter 13), and the time types, which the country module ships and which say how each kind of hour is paid (Chapter 14). Notice the Changes lines: the records change at very different speeds. A parameter changes every year; a rule only when the method changes; a structure type almost never. Keeping each fact in the record that changes at its speed is what turns a new tax year into a data update instead of a rewrite. Common pitfall: fixing one employee in a shared rule A rule is shared by every employee on its structures. Editing the ONSS rule because one employee's line looks wrong changes everyone's payslips, and stops the rule from receiving Odoo's fixes (Chapter 21). Look for the cause in that employee's version, worked days or inputs first.

p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
x: Everything in the next three chapters follows from five decisions. 1 · Rules are data A rule is a record with a small formula, not a program. Countries ship rules as data; customers add their own from the screen; one engine runs them all. Wheresalary rules and structuresChapter 19 2 · Legal numbers live in dated parameters A rule asks for "the cap" by its code and gets the value valid on the payslip's date. Next year's law is a new value, never an edit. Whererule parametersChapters 11, 21 3 · Time is computed, not stored Work entries are derived from the schedule and time off whenever a payslip needs them, so a late change of leave is never forgotten. Wherework entries and worked daysChapter 14 4 · Totals connect the rules Rules do not call each other. Each one adds to running totals (gross, taxable base, net), and later rules read the totals. Wheresalary categoriesChapter 20 5 · Countries are layers on a shared framework The engine, payslips, pay runs, accounting and declarations are shared. A country module adds rules, parameters, categories, fields and its filings on top, and never replaces the engine. Wherecountry modules l10n_xx_hr_payrollChapters 9, 22 Around the world The same five records carry very different laws: Mexico: one structure type, two structures (regular pay and the Christmas bonus), frequencies from weekly to monthly. Belgium: about ten structures for one structure type, because holiday pay, the 13th month and termination are separate payslips. India: a second structure type for interns. United States: one structure holding the income-tax rule of every state; each rule's condition tests the employee's work address. Netherlands: a small module that is almost only data. Review checklist Before reviewing a payroll database or a country module, sort its records by owner: Ships with the country module and is updated by Odoo: structure types, structures, rules, categories, parameters and their values, the payroll settings of time types, dashboard warnings. Belongs to the customer: employees and their versions, time off, inputs, company settings, and any rule or structure they created (Odoo marks those as created by a user). A shipped record the customer edited no longer receives Odoo's updates (Chapter 21). List them; each one needs a reason. A legal number typed in a customer record, or a customer-specific amount in a shipped rule, is in the wrong place.

p: Chapter 18 · The engine in one picture
x: The payroll engine turns one employee's version, time and inputs for one period into payslip lines, by applying the rules of one structure in order. Accounting, declarations and reports read the lines; they never recompute. Rules are data: small formulas stored as records, shipped by country modules or created by users, run by one engine that fits on a page. Each line is amount × quantity × rate ÷ 100, and its total is added to the rule's categories for later rules. Five records decide a payslip: structure type, structure, salary rule, salary category, rule parameter. They change at different speeds, from almost never to every year. The country module owns the configuration; the customer owns versions, time and inputs; a shipped record the customer edited stops receiving updates.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A structure is a list of rules for one kind of payslip; a rule is one line, with a condition, an amount and a place in the order Explain what a structure is, why a country has several, and how a payslip finds its own Read any salary rule: its code, condition, amount, categories and position Say what a rule can read, what it cannot, and what it is allowed to do Explain why the order of the rules carries meaning Recognise the three shapes of rule and review each one Jurgen and Mélanie are paid on the same structure, Monthly Pay. Yet Jurgen's February payslip has a low-wage bonus line that Mélanie's lacks, and Marie's has a company-car line that neither of them has. Nobody added or removed those lines by hand: the structure holds every rule, and each rule decides for itself, payslip by payslip, whether it applies.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A salary structure (also pay structure) is a named list of salary rules for one kind of payslip. When a payslip is computed, the engine runs the rules of its structure, and only those. Three things follow: One structure per kind of payslip. A regular month, a 13th month, holiday pay and a leaver's indemnity are taxed and declared differently, so each is a separate payslip on its own structure. A rule can belong to several structures. The social-security rule of a country is usually shared by its regular and bonus structures; it is one record, maintained once. Structures are grouped by structure type. The type (the kind of pay on the employee's version) lists its structures and names the default one, for the regular payslip. Regular Mélanie's version → its structure type: CP200 BE → the type's default: Monthly Pay Special a pay run or a payslip created on purpose → a structure chosen for it → 13th Month, Double Holidays, Termination Fees… Either way, a payslip has exactly one structure, and only that structure's rules run. A regular pay run takes each employee's default structure from the version. For a payment outside the regular month, you create a run (or a single off-cycle payslip) and choose its structure (Chapter 15). Country Structures Why so many, or so few Belgium ten: Monthly Pay, Double Holidays, 13th Month, Termination Fees, two exit holiday-pay structures, Advance Pay, and three bonus plans each has its own withholding method or declaration code Mexico two: Regular Pay, Christmas Bonus the bonus has an exempt part and its own tax Most other countries one regular structure bonuses are lines on the regular payslip Common pitfall: a rule missing from one structure A rule runs only on the structures it is attached to. A new allowance added to Monthly Pay but not to Termination Fees is simply absent from leavers' final pay, with no error. When you add or review a rule, check its structures list.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A salary rule computes at most one line of the payslip. Every rule, in every country, answers the same five questions. Here is the Belgian employee social-security rule, as you can open it under Configuration > Salary > Rules: Social contributionONSS 1Identity name and codeThe code is how other rules refer to its result (result_rules['ONSS']), and the code on the payslip line. 2When condition, Python: result = not version.no_onss and not version.is_PFI()Always present, except for the few employees exempt from social security. Other choices: always, an input is present, a domain. 3How much amount = the contribution base (a total, ONSS_BASE); rate = −13.07 %, read from dated ratesOther choices: a fixed amount, a percentage of a total, the amount of an input. 4Where it goes categories: the running net, the taxable base, the social-security total; partner: the social security office; shown on the payslip: alwaysAccounts sit on the rule too, when the country maps them. 5Order sequence 600After the gross salary lines, before the taxable salary (GROSS, 1000) and the tax. Mélanie, February 2026 amount4,000.00 × quantity1 × rate−13.07 % = total−522.80 The line shows all four numbers, so anyone can check it without opening the rule. The same rule in Odoo. ① its code and its sequence. ② its categories. ③ the amount code: the rate comes from a helper that reads the downloaded rates. ④ a Belgian addition: the sectors the rule does not apply to. Two details of the card matter in review. The rate is not written in the rule: it comes from dated parameters (Chapter 21), so a new rate next year needs no rule change. And the rule feeds three totals at once, which is how one contribution lowers both the net and the taxable base (Chapter 20).

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A rule's formula runs with a dictionary of names, the same in every country. The list is short and stable: What Name in the rule Example The employee, the version, the company employee, version, company version.wage The payslip and its period payslip payslip.date_to Time worked this period worked_days worked_days['WORK100'].number_of_days Amounts typed for this period inputs inputs['COMMISSIONS'].amount Totals so far categories categories['GROSS'] Results of earlier rules result_rules result_rules['SBC']['total'] Legal values on the payslip's date payslip._rule_parameter(code) payslip._rule_parameter('l10n_mx_uma') The form of every rule lists these names next to the code editor (the right side of the screenshot above). A country module can add a few of its own; the Belgian one adds the employee's earlier payslips of the year. What a rule cannot read is a rule that comes later. At its turn, a later rule has not run yet, and its total, or a category only it feeds, reads as 0, without any error. The same silence hides a misspelt category code. By contrast, worked_days and inputs only contain the codes present on this payslip: reading inputs['BONUS'] when no bonus was typed stops the computation with an error. That is why input rules start by checking (result = 'BONUS' in inputs), or use the Input Value condition, which does it for them.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A rule produces one line or none. Nothing else. Condition true: the rule returns an amount, a quantity (default 1) and a rate (default 100 %), and may rename its line. The engine stores one line: amount × quantity × rate ÷ 100. A total of zero is still a line; the rule's Visibility setting decides whether it is printed. Condition false: no line at all. Its code is absent from the payslip, its totals receive nothing, and later rules read 0 for it. A rule does not change records. It does not write on the employee, create a leave or update a balance; those are actions of the payslip's validation or of other modules. Rule code runs in a restricted interpreter (no imports), but it can still reach the database through the records it reads, which is why only payroll managers may edit rules, and why a rule that writes anything is a review finding. Worked example: Marie's meal vouchers Marie received 20 meal vouchers in February. The rule Retain on Meal Voucher returns amount 1.09 € (the employee's share of one voucher: face value minus the employer's part, both on her version), quantity 20 (one voucher per day worked) and rate −100 %. Total: 1.09 × 20 × −100 % = −21.80 €. The payslip line reads "20 × 1.09", which the employee can check without asking anyone.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: Rules run in the order of their sequence number. There is no other dependency mechanism: a rule sees exactly what ran before it. So the order of a structure is not cosmetic; it is the law's order of operations. BASICbasic salary 1 → ONSSsocial security 600 → GROSStaxable salary 1000 → P.Pwithholding tax 1400 → NETnet salary 3340 → Employercontributions 4000+ knows: the worked days + the basic salary + the contribution + the taxable base + the tax: everything the employee gets + the net; changes nothing the employee gets first rule: knows only the version, time and inputslast rule: knows every earlier line The Belgian monthly structure, read as a timeline. Each rule can use what the rules on its left produced: Contributions before tax. In Belgium, as in many countries, the taxable base is the salary after the employee's social security, so the contribution must run first. Net last among the employee's lines, because it sums them all. Employer contributions after the net. They are a cost for the company, not a deduction from the employee; running them after the net makes it obvious they cannot change it. (Some countries run them earlier, and keep them out of the net by category instead: Chapter 20.) The numbers themselves mean nothing: Mexico uses 1 to 210, Belgium 1 to over 6,000. Do not memorise them; read them relative to their neighbours, and leave gaps when you create rules so the next law fits in between. Common pitfall: reading a total that is filled later A rule at sequence 500 that reads categories['GROSS'], filled at 1000, gets 0 and computes a wrong line silently. When a line is unexpectedly zero, compare the sequence of the rule with the sequences of the rules that feed what it reads.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: Open any country's rules and you find three shapes. 1 · No code A fixed amount, or a percentage of a total, chosen in the form. Fits an employer's own simple rule. Anyone can read it. 2 · Input rule The amount is typed on the payslip or the employee for this period. Fits commissions, bonuses, one-off deductions. The rule is also the input type. 3 · Formula A few lines of Python reading totals, time and parameters. Fits contributions, taxes, caps. Most rules of a country module. No code. A customer who pays a company pension contribution of 3 % of the basic salary needs no developer: Amount Type "Percentage (%)", based on categories['BASIC'], 3 %, condition "Always Present", category "Deduction", attached to the regular structure. (An illustrative rule; country modules rarely use this shape, because their rates belong in dated parameters.) Input rule. Mexico's COMMISSIONS has condition and amount both set to Input Value: the line exists only when someone types a commission on the payslip, and its amount is what was typed. It belongs to the category Taxable Allowance, so commissions are taxed, and it is shown only when not zero. There is no separate "input type" record: the rule is the input type, and its code is the key in inputs. Formula reading a parameter. Mexico's additional sickness-and-maternity quota (employee part) is due on the part of the daily contribution base above three times the UMA, the official reference unit: base_contribution_salary = result_rules['SBC']['total'] daily_uma = payslip._rule_parameter('l10n_mx_uma')['daily'] result = max(0, (base_contribution_salary - 3 * daily_uma)) result_qty = days_without_disabilities result_rate = -0.4 It reads an earlier result (SBC, sequence 124, before this rule at 136), a dated parameter (the UMA) and sets amount, quantity and rate separately, so the line explains itself: daily excess × days × −0.4 %. A reviewer would still note one thing: the 0.4 % rate is written in the code while the UMA is a parameter. If the law changes the rate, this rule changes, and so would every old payslip recomputed with it. Around the world: switching rules on and off Conditions are how one structure serves very different employees: United States: one income-tax rule per state, each with result = version.address_id.state_id.code == 'CA' (or its own state). India: income tax is withheld only in the months the rule's condition selects. Mexico: commissions and bonuses appear only when an input is typed. Belgium: a filter in front of every condition skips the rules of other sectors (joint committees), so one structure serves them all. Review checklist For each rule you create or review: No legal number in the code. Rates, caps and brackets come from a parameter (Chapter 21); a literal 0.4 or 25 * is a finding. Everything it reads is computed earlier. Each category and result it reads is fed by rules with a lower sequence. It feeds the right totals. A rule with no category, or a missing one, never reaches the gross, the taxable base or the net (Chapter 20). It checks inputs and time codes exist before reading them, or uses the Input Value condition. It rounds where the law rounds, and only there. The engine does not round inside a computation; Belgium's withholding rule, for instance, rounds the monthly tax down to the cent itself. It is on every structure where it applies, and changes no record.

p: Chapter 19 · Structures and rules
x: A structure is a named list of rules for one kind of payslip; a country has one per payslip that is taxed or declared differently. A payslip gets its structure from the version's structure type (the default), or from the pay run or off-cycle payslip that names one. A rule answers five questions: identity (name, code), when (condition), how much (amount × quantity × rate), where it goes (categories, accounts, visibility) and order (sequence). A rule reads the employee and version, the payslip, worked days, inputs, totals so far, earlier results and parameters; never a later rule, which reads as 0. A rule produces one line or none, and changes no record. Order is meaning: contributions before tax, net last, employer contributions after the net. Three shapes: no code, input rule, formula reading a parameter.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
h: Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: Running totals that rules add to and later rules read: the gross, the bases, the net Define a salary category as a running total, and say why rules read totals rather than each other Walk the standard chain BASIC → ALW → GROSS → DED → NET, with employer contributions outside the net Explain how one rule feeds several totals, with Marie's company car Say who reads categories after the payslip is computed Check that a country's categories match its legal bases Belgium adds a new tax-free allowance. The social-security rule, the withholding rule and the net rule do not change: the new rule simply joins the right totals, and every rule that reads those totals sees it. That is the whole point of categories: rules never name each other; they meet in shared totals.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: A salary category (salary rule category in Odoo) is a named running total. Each rule adds its result to its categories; later rules read the total instead of naming every rule that fed it. Categories are how rules talk to each other. Three things follow: A new rule needs no change elsewhere. Put a new allowance in the allowances total, and the gross and the net pick it up. One rule can feed several totals. A contribution can lower both the net and the taxable base. A total is not a line. It lives during the computation. When the law needs it on the payslip, a rule copies it into a line (that is what the GROSS rule does). Rules add… Basic salary3,000 Transport allowance100 Phone allowance50 Pension contribution−150 Income tax−400 → …to running totals BASIC3,000 ALW (allowances)100 + 50 = 150 DED (deductions)−150 − 400 = −550 → …that later rules read Net ruleBASIC + ALW + DED 3,000 + 150 − 550 = 2,600 A third allowance would change nothing here. Illustrative numbers. The net rule names three totals, not five rules.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: The payroll framework ships seven categories, and every country starts from them. Five form a chain from the basic salary to the net: BASICpay for the time worked and paidcomes first: everything else derives from it → ALWallowances: everything paid on top of basicearnings that are not time → GROSS"Taxable Salary": basic + allowances so fara snapshot taken before taxes are computed on it → DEDdeductions: contributions, tax, garnishmentseverything that lowers the net → NETbasic + allowances + deductionswhat the bank transfer pays COMP (company contribution): the employer's contributions. Recorded, booked and declared, but outside the chain: the net formula never reads it, because the employee does not pay them. EXTRA_HOURS: overtime pay, kept apart so a country can treat it differently (for example, exclude it from the hours that set the hourly rate). Two words decide where a rule lands: its category and its position. Key idea: category and position GROSS is "taxable" by position. It reads BASIC + ALW at the moment it runs. An expense reimbursement is in ALW too, but runs after GROSS: the net includes it, the taxable salary does not. An expense paid back is not salary. Garnishments come after taxes because the law protects a part of the net (Chapter 6); the seizable amount is known only once taxes are withheld. Employer contributions stay out of the net by category, not by position. The net reads BASIC, ALW and DED, never COMP, wherever the employer rules run.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: Before any rule runs, each worked-days line adds its amount to the categories of its time type (Chapter 14). Attendance usually feeds BASIC; a paid leave type feeds what the country decides; unpaid leave is worth 0 and adds nothing. That is how time reaches the totals: the basic salary rule often just reads categories['BASIC']. Common pitfall: a paid time type with no category If a paid time type has no category, its amount is on the worked-days line but never reaches BASIC, so the gross and the net miss it. When a country adds a time type, check its categories. The opposite mistake also exists: a rule that both reads a total seeded by worked days and writes into it counts the amount twice.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
h: One rule, several totals: Marie's company car
x: Belgian law needs three bases, not one: the running net (what will be paid), the contribution base (what social security is computed on) and the taxable base. So Belgium keeps one total per base, and each rule says which bases it belongs to. Marie's company car is a benefit in kind: taxed as if it were salary, but never paid in cash (Chapter 2). Its rule, ATN.CAR, adds 136.77 € to the taxable base and nothing to the running net. The social-security rule adds its −980.25 € to both. Marie, February 2026 Line total Running net Taxable base Worked days (attendance) 7,500.00 7,500.00 ONSS social security, 13.07 % −980.25 6,519.75 6,519.75 ATN.CAR company car 136.77 6,519.75 6,656.52 GROSS reads the taxable base 6,656.52 The car changes the tax, not the cash: 7,500.00 − 980.25 + 136.77 = 6,656.52 € of taxable salary. The withholding rule, the net rule and the declarations never mention the car; they read totals. A new benefit in kind next year will be one more rule in the taxable base. Worked example: Mélanie's three bases Mélanie has no benefit in kind. Her social security (−522.80 €) lowers the running net and the taxable base but not the contribution base, which stays at 4,000.00 €. So her GROSS line, the taxable salary, is 3,477.20 €, not 4,000.00 €. After withholding (−826.69 €) and a special contribution (−36.24 €), the net rule reads the running net: 2,614.27 €.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: A category can have a parent. When a rule adds to a category, the engine also adds to its parent, and to the parent's parent. A country can then make the generic chain more precise without rewriting it. ALW · allowancesread by the net rule TAXABLE_ALWcommissions, bonuses: read by GROSS exempt allowancesadded to ALW directly: in the net, not taxed DED · deductionsread by the net rule IMSS_EMPLOYEEemployee social security income tax (ISR)added to DED directly Mexico, as shipped. Its two formulas: # GROSS, the taxable salary: only the taxable allowances result = categories['BASIC'] + categories['TAXABLE_ALW'] # NET: unchanged from the standard; the children roll up into ALW and DED result = categories['BASIC'] + categories['ALW'] + categories['DED'] The net formula is the generic one, yet it sees commissions and employee social security, because their categories roll up into ALW and DED. The taxable salary reads only the child, so exempt allowances stay out of it.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
h: Who reads categories after the payslip
x: Categories exist during the computation; afterwards, each line remembers its rule, and the rule its categories. That is enough for everything downstream: Who Reads Declarations and yearly certificates the sum of a category over a period, across validated payslips: the taxable base of the quarter, the tax withheld in the year (Chapter 17) Payroll reports payslip lines grouped by rule or by category The journal entry each rule's accounts, not its categories (Chapter 16) The payslip's gross and net fields the lines with codes BASIC, GROSS, NET In practice If a declaration total is wrong while every payslip looks right, look for a rule in the wrong category. A declaration sums categories, so designing a country's categories is designing its declarations: start from the boxes of the forms.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: The rule of thumb: one category per legal base. Whatever amount the law computes something on (a contribution base, a taxable base, a pensionable salary) gets its own total, and each rule says which bases it belongs to. Countries keep the codes BASIC, GROSS and NET, because the payslip fields and reports read them, and add what their law needs between them. Around the world Mexico keeps the generic tree, adds child categories (TAXABLE_ALW, IMSS_EMPLOYEE) and a separate total for the social-security base, SBC, capped by its own rule. India keeps the generic formulas: GROSS = BASIC + ALW, so there GROSS really is the gross salary. Belgium uses a running net: one total (REMUNERATION_BASE) that every rule paying or withholding cash feeds, plus a contribution base and a taxable base. The net rule just reads the running net. United States keeps pre-tax deductions in their own category, because they lower the taxable wages. Common pitfall: GROSS does not mean the same everywhere The GROSS category is labelled Taxable Salary. In India it is the gross; in Mexico, the taxable part of the earnings; in Belgium, the salary after employee social security (Mélanie: 3,477.20 €, not 4,000.00 €). Before comparing "gross" across countries, or building a report on it, open the GROSS rule and read its formula. Review checklist Every legal base has a category: list the bases in the law (contribution base, taxable base, pensionable pay…) and find each one. Each rule feeds exactly the bases the law says: for every earning, ask "is it subject to contributions? to tax? paid in cash?" and compare with its categories. Is GROSS gross or taxable here? Read the formula, and check the reports and declarations that use it agree. Every paid time type has a category, and no rule both reads and writes the same seeded total. Employer contributions are outside the net by category, whatever their position.

p: Chapter 20 · Categories: how rules talk to each other
x: A category is a named running total: rules add to it, later rules read it, and rules never name each other. The standard chain is BASIC → ALW → GROSS (taxable salary) → DED → NET; employer contributions (COMP) stay outside the net. Category decides which totals a rule changes; position decides which rules see it. A reimbursement after GROSS is paid but not taxed. Worked days add their amounts to their time types' categories before the first rule. One rule can feed several totals: Marie's car is in the taxable base, not in the running net. Parent categories roll up, so a country can refine the chain without changing the net formula. Declarations sum categories over a period; one category per legal base is the design rule.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: Dated legal values, how Odoo's fixes reach every customer, what to do when data is not enough, and how to prove the result Explain a rule parameter and predict which value a payslip reads Decide where a value belongs: parameter, company setting, version field or rule Explain how country updates reach customers, and what happens to a record the customer edited Choose the lightest extension when data is not enough Prove a localization works with golden payslips frozen as tests On 1 January the minimum wage, a tax scale and a contribution cap change. Nobody touches a rule. Odoo adds three dated values to the country's data, every customer database receives them within a week, and the first January payslip reads them, while a December payslip recomputed in February still reads December's law. This chapter shows how, and what to do when the law asks for more than a new number.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: A rule parameter is a code with a list of dated values: a rate, a cap, a tax scale, each valid from a date until the next value starts. A rule never contains the number itself; it asks for the parameter by its code, and the payslip gets the value valid on its own date. Next year's law is a new value, never an edit. Three things follow: History is kept. Old values stay, so any past payslip recomputes with the law of its period (Chapter 11). A value has a start date only. It lasts until the next one; a temporary measure is two values, the measure and the return to normal. A value can be any shape the rule needs: a number, a list of brackets, a table per frequency. Keep the same shape every year, so the rule never needs to know the year. from 01/01/20221,270 from 01/01/20231,260 from 01/01/20241,300 from 01/01/20251,350 from 01/01/20261,400 June 2024 payslip (1–30 June) reads 1,300 An illustrative parameter minimum_wage with five values. The June 2024 payslip asks for it: payslip._rule_parameter('minimum_wage') # 1300 The rule is simple: the value with the latest start date on or before the payslip's end date. For June 2024 that is the value of 1 January 2024. Note the 2023 value is lower than 2022's: values follow the law, not a trend, and nobody edits the old ones to "fix" them. Belgium's cap on the flat-rate professional expenses works exactly like this: 5,930 € from 1 January 2025, 6,070 € from 1 January 2026. Mélanie's February 2026 payslip reads 6,070; a December 2025 payslip recomputed today still reads 5,930. A Belgian parameter, Work Bonus: Coefficient. ① its code, which rules use to read it. ②–⑥ five values dated in 2026, newest first; older values stay below, so any past payslip recomputes with its own law. Common pitfall: a period that straddles a date One value applies to the whole payslip, read at its end date. A weekly payslip from 29 June to 5 July reads the July value for the whole week. When the law requires splitting, the rule must ask twice, with two reference dates, and prorate.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: Not every number is a parameter. Ask who decides it, and for whom. Who decides this value? The law a rule parameter, dated tax scales, contribution rates, caps, the minimum wage The employer, for everyone a company setting Mexico: the company's income-tax calculation method; Belgium: the employer's sector The person's situation a field on the version wage, family situation, company car, a fixed allowance agreed with this employee The method a rule (or a helper it calls) how the tax is computed from the scale, in what order Each kind of value has its own date: the parameter's start date, the version's date, the company setting's date. Rules have none. The last column is the subtle one: rules are not dated. Change a rule and every payslip you recompute afterwards uses the new method, including old ones. So a rule should be written to be valid for every year it supports, and everything that changes by year must sit in a parameter it reads.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: Country data is not frozen at installation. Odoo keeps improving it, and delivers it without a module upgrade. 1The law changesa new rate from 1 January, a corrected rule → 2Odoo adds itin the country module's data files: a new dated value, or the fixed rule → 3A weekly job reloadsthe scheduled action “Payroll: Update data” reloads every country's payroll data into every database → 4Next payslipreads the new value at its date, or runs the fixed rule Untouched record: updated every week, with nothing to do. Record the customer edited: flagged as manually updated and skipped by the weekly job, until someone clicks Reset. Why the protection? A customer may have a reason to change what a rule computes, and a weekly reload must not silently undo it. So when a user edits a shipped rule's computation (its code, condition, amount, categories, structures or sequence; not its label), or edits a shipped parameter, Odoo marks the record and stops updating it. Time types are protected the same way. Records the customer created from scratch are never touched by the update. A Belgian rule edited by a user. ① the banner: the rule will no longer be updated. ② Reset reloads the standard version, drops the manual changes and resumes the updates. On a parameter, Reset also removes the values users added. Worked example: a customer patches a cap MyVidangeCompany's payroll officer thinks the 2026 professional-expenses cap is wrong and edits it "until Odoo fixes it". The parameter is now flagged. When Odoo ships the 2027 value, the weekly job skips this parameter: January 2027 payslips silently keep reading the 2026 cap. The right move was to report the value; once the record is flagged, Reset brings back Odoo's values and the updates. In practice In a review or a support case, search the rules and parameters flagged as manually updated. Each one is a place where the customer stopped receiving the law's changes. Ask why; if the reason is gone, reset it. If the customer needs a different computation for good, a rule of their own next to the standard one is easier to maintain than an edited standard rule.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: Most of a localization is data: parameters, rules, categories, time types, warnings. Sometimes the law needs more. Climb the ladder only as far as needed. lighter heavier 1 · A recorddata a parameter, a rule, a category, a time type, a dashboard warningupdated weekly, resettable, readable by a payroll expert 2 · A field on the versiondata about the person a fact the law needs about the employee, which rules then readBelgium: family situation, company car 3 · A helper the rules callPython method a formula too long for a rule; the rule stays one lineIndia: the yearly income-tax projection 4 · An engine hookguarded by country change one step of the engine for one country onlyBelgium: round every line to the cent; Mexico: value worked days from a legal daily salary 5 · Patch the enginefor one country neverevery future engine change would break that country, or every other one Each rung is harder to change and to review than the one above. A record can be changed by a payroll expert and is delivered by the weekly job; a helper or a hook needs a developer and a code release. Rung 4 always starts with a country guard, because one database can hold a Belgian and a Mexican company: def _get_payslip_line_total(self, amount, quantity, rate, rule): total = super()._get_payslip_line_total(amount, quantity, rate, rule) if self.company_id.country_id.code != 'BE': return total return float_round(total, precision_rounding=0.01, rounding_method='HALF-UP') Belgium's line rounding: other countries get the standard total untouched. Chapter 22 lists the few hooks a new localization actually needs. Key idea Before writing Python, ask: "could a payroll officer need to change this next year?" If yes (a rate, a cap, a list of codes), it belongs in a record.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: A payslip can be wrong by one cent for years before anyone notices. The proof is a set of golden payslips (Chapter 10): payslips computed independently of Odoo, from the law and the administration's examples, and frozen as automated tests. Each test sets up an employee, computes a payslip for a period, and compares every line with the expected amount: def test_standard_month(self): payslip = self._generate_payslip(date(2026, 2, 1), date(2026, 2, 28)) self._validate_payslip(payslip, { 'BASIC': 4000.0, 'ONSS': -522.80, 'GROSS': 3477.20, 'P.P': -826.69, 'NET': 2614.27, }) Illustrative, with Mélanie's February 2026 values. The tests run on every change to the module, so a fix for one case cannot silently break another. Write a test… Because Case study per situation the law distinguishes each one takes a different path through the rules Mélanie (standard), Jurgen (low wage), Marie (car, family) per special time absences, joiners and overtime hide bugs better than arithmetic Yannick joins on 12 March; Jurgen's April per extra structure each kind of payslip has its own rules Emma's exit payslips on both sides of every date change proves the new value starts on the right day, and the old one still applies before Jurgen's low-wage threshold, March and April 2026 above every cap and in the top bracket a cap that is never reached is never tested Marie Tests run on fixed dates, so a test of 2025 keeps checking the 2025 law forever. When you add next year's values, keep the old tests unchanged: if one fails, an old value was edited instead of a new one added. And break the module on purpose once (multiply a cap by ten): if no test fails, the suite has a hole. Common pitfall: expected values copied from Odoo A test whose expected amounts were produced by the code it tests proves nothing about the law; it can only detect a change. The first expected value of each case must come from an independent calculation, with its source in a comment. Around the world Mexico reads the UMA and the tax tables from dated parameters, with one table per pay frequency. Belgium downloads social-security rates every day into dated parameters, one per employer class and worker type. Switzerland imports tax tariffs from official files through a wizard. United States builds a parameter code per state for unemployment insurance rates, so a new state is a new parameter, not new code. Review checklist New values are added, not edited. Each yearly change is a new dated value; old values and old tests are untouched. Every legal number is a parameter, with a code prefixed by the country (l10n_xx_…): codes are shared by all countries. Customer edits are known: rules and parameters flagged as manually updated are listed and justified. Code is guarded by country, and sits on the lightest rung of the ladder that works. A test per new case: each new situation, structure or dated value comes with a golden payslip, on both sides of its date.

p: Chapter 21 · Parameters, updates and safe extensions
x: A rule parameter is a code with dated values; a payslip reads the value with the latest start date on or before its end date. Next year's law is a new value, never an edit. Law goes in parameters, the employer's choices in company settings, the person's facts on the version, the method in rules. Rules are not dated. A weekly job reloads every country's payroll data, so new values and fixes arrive without an upgrade; a record the customer edited is flagged and skipped until Reset. When data is not enough, climb the ladder: record, version field, helper, country-guarded hook; never patch the engine for one country. Golden payslips frozen as tests are the proof: one per legal situation, per structure, on both sides of every date, above every cap.

p: Chapter 22 · A template for any localization, and how to review one
x: A payroll localization (also country module, l10n module) is the country layer of Chapter 9: one or two Odoo modules, l10n_xx_hr_payroll and l10n_xx_hr_payroll_account, that turn one country's payroll law into records and a little Python on top of the shared engine.
